activity: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
knowledge_domain: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
fact: In jazz and blues jams, players often 'trade fours', taking turns to improvise four bars each.
story:
Dominic had memorized the twelve-bar progression until he could hear it in his sleep, but every time the recording reached the turnaround, his fingers froze on the frets of his borrowed guitar. He wanted one solo, just one, that didn't sound like he was reading it off a page. The music room was empty after school except for the sound of someone playing trumpet in the practice room next door, and the wall between them was so thin that the notes seemed to dissolve through it, bending and smearing in a way his own playing never did.

The trumpet stopped, and Louis stuck his head around the door. "Was that you butchering the B flat?" he asked, grinning. He came in carrying his trumpet case like a briefcase, dropped onto the piano bench, and set up without asking. "I've been stuck on the same thing for a week. I can play the changes, but it's all scales. It's like talking in spelling words."

Dominic plucked the low E string. "Mr. Fitzgerald says we're supposed to be able to answer each other, like a conversation. But I don't even know how to start a sentence." He played the first four bars of the progression, then stopped. "Wait. Four bars. What if we split it up? You take four, I take four, back and forth."

Louis frowned at him. "That's not really how a solo works. You're supposed to take the whole thing yourself." But he raised the trumpet anyway. "Fine. But I go first, because you'll need time to think of something."

He played four bars, and it wasn't spelling words at all. It was a question, a short rising phrase that ended hanging in the air. Dominic's hands were sweating. He didn't try to answer with something clever; he just took the last three notes Louis had played and bent them lower, the way he'd heard through the wall. Louis sat up straight. "Okay, that's an answer. My turn." He took Dominic's bent note and pushed it higher, faster. They went around the progression twice, each four-bar turn stealing from the last one, and by the end Dominic was laughing so hard he missed a chord change and neither of them cared.

"That thing we were doing," Louis said, wiping the trumpet's bell with his shirt. "Trading fours. Brian told me about it after jazz band. He says that's how the players do it at the Friday jam downtown." He paused. "I thought I had to do it alone, the whole solo. I was wrong about that."

Mr. Fitzgerald looked in from the hallway, keys jangling like a permanent tenant of the corridor was finally heading home. "Lock up when you're done," he said, then listened for a moment. "Same time tomorrow?"

"Same time tomorrow," Dominic said, and turned the amp back on.

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: According to the U.S. Fire Administration, failing to clean the dryer is the leading factor in home clothes dryer fires, because built-up lint blocks the airflow and lets heat collect.
story:
Jake's lucky jersey was in the bottom of his laundry basket, grass-stained and smelling like Saturday's game, and he needed it clean by tomorrow morning for the team photo. His mom had left for the night shift, so the job was his. He sorted the pile on his bedroom floor into three hills: darks, whites, and a small hopeful heap of reds he decided to wash alone so nothing would bleed. He measured the detergent the way the bottle showed, turned the dial to warm, and sat on the washer lid while the drum thumped through its cycle.

When the wash ended, he hauled the wet clothes to the dryer, stuffed them in, and punched the button. He had forty minutes before he wanted to be in bed. He played a game on his phone, checked the clock, and came back to find the dryer still turning and the jersey still damp. He ran it again. Another forty minutes passed, and it was still damp, though the machine felt warm as a toaster on the outside. His stomach tightened a little. If it wasn't dry by eleven, he would be folding a wet jersey over a chair and hoping.

He stood in front of the dryer with his arms crossed, thinking. The drum spun. The heat was there. So what was missing? He pressed his palm against the back of the machine, then crouched down and noticed the panel near the floor was pushed in perpendicular to the wall instead of flush against it, like someone had kicked it crooked. That was a clue, but a small one. The bigger question was where the hot air was going, because air wasn't something he could watch move. He would have to find where it left the machine.

He pulled out the plastic filter under the lid of the door, and a thick grey mat of lint came with it, felted like a scavenger's nest, dense enough to hold its shape in his hand. He peeled it off and held the filter up to the kitchen light. The mesh was still half plugged with fuzz, a second layer he scraped loose with his fingernail. He washed the filter under the tap, snapped it back in, and restarted the dryer, and this time the machine made a sound he hadn't heard before, a steady rush like breath. Twenty minutes later the jersey came out dry and warm and smelling of clean cotton.

He texted Fraser, who was always good for weird facts. When Fraser called back, Jake read him what he had found while waiting. "It says here that according to the U.S. Fire Administration, failing to clean the dryer is the leading factor in home clothes dryer fires, because built-up lint blocks the airflow and lets heat collect."

"Dude," Fraser said. "You almost burned your house down for a jersey."

"It says leading factor," Jake said. "That means number one." He looked at the grey mat of lint, which he had set on the counter like evidence. He folded his jersey carefully, sleeves in first, exactly the way his mom did, and set it on top of the basket. Then he taped a strip of paper above the dryer that said "JAKE" in block letters, and underlined it twice.

activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
knowledge_domain: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
fact: Universal indicator changes to a range of different colours, and each colour matches a different pH number on a chart.
story:
The third graders kept asking Jaxon the same question, and his litmus paper kept giving them the same useless answer. "Is it acid?" a girl in a dinosaur hoodie asked again, pointing at his bottle of mystery liquid. The paper had turned red, which meant acid, yes, but she wanted more than that. She wanted a number.

"A number?" Jaxon said. "It's paper. Paper doesn't do numbers."

"You have a chart," she said, jabbing a finger at his poster, where he had drawn the whole pH scale from zero to fourteen. "So what's this one?"

He looked at his poster, then at the red strip, then at the poster again. Litmus was meticulous about one thing and stubborn about everything else. It would tell you acid or base and then basically shrug. He had seven solutions lined up on his table, and two of them were supposed to be close, a weak acid and a strong one, and he could not tell which strip was redder. One girl had insisted both his soapy solution and his baking soda solution were "the same poison," and he could not prove otherwise with a strip that just said base, base.

Jaxen wandered over from the neighbouring table, chewing a pretzel. "Mr. Nkosi says you should've done volcanoes."

"Mr. Nkosi also insulate d his coffee mug with a sock," Jaxon said. "I'm not taking tips from him."

"That was actually pretty smart," said Gregory, who was at the volcano table and had no loyalty.

Jaxon stared at his row of strips. The dinosaur girl had moved on to Gregory's table and was interrogating him instead, which stung. He had drawn a pH chart and he had nothing to measure it with. It was a contradiction he could not talk his way out of: a scale with no ruler.

Then he saw the little bottle at the back of his supply box, the one Mr. Nkosi had handed him last week with the words "backup plan" and nothing else. Universal indicator, the label said. He'd ignored it because the litmus had seemed simpler. He dropped a few drops into a cup of his first solution and swirled it. The liquid went orange.

"Orange," the dinosaur girl said, reappearing at his elbow like she'd never left. She grabbed his chart and ran her finger down it. "That's pH three."

He tried the soapy one. Green. She checked the chart again. "Eight."

"Universal indicator changes to a whole range of different colours," Jaxon said slowly, watching the baking soda cup settle into blue, "and every colour matches a different pH number on the chart." The strong acid came out red, the weak one orange, and the two strips that had looked identical suddenly lived on opposite ends of a rainbow.

Mr. Nkosi strolled by with his sock-wrapped mug. "Backup plan," he said, and kept walking.

The girl was already dripping indicator into her own juice box.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Muscles grow stronger during recovery after training, not during the workout itself, so rest days are part of getting better.
story:
"Laurence, you look like a caribou crossing the tundra," Adelaide called from the bleachers, "and I mean the slow one at the back of the herd."

Laurence shuffled through her layup drills and bricked the shot off the backboard. That was the third brick in a row, and it was Tuesday, which meant she had now done full practice every single day for eleven straight days. Her legs felt like wet sand.

"Very funny," she said. "Your jokes signify nothing."

"They signify that you used to beat Eddie in sprints and yesterday he lapped you." Eddie waved cheerfully from the free throw line, where he was lapping her again, just to make the point.

At lunch Laurence spread her week out on the table like a detective. Monday, sprints. Tuesday, sprints. Wednesday, sprints, plus two hundred shots before school. Thursday she had skipped the two hundred shots but kept the sprints because skipping felt like quitting, and quitting was for people who liked being slow. She had done everything right, more than right, and she was getting slower. That made no sense. Unless the thing making her better was not the practicing itself.

She flipped her notebook to a blank page and wrote: What if you don't get better AT practice? She stared at it. Every day she trained, then trained again the next morning, no gaps. Eddie, who was suddenly fast, took two days off a week to go to his grandma's. Coincidence? Laurence did not believe in coincidences, only in clues.

She ran an experiment, and she hated it. Saturday she stayed home, sprawled on the couch, watching her teammates through the gym window like a sad raccoon. Sunday, more couch. "This is the worst plan I've ever had," she texted Adelaide.

"It's not a plan, it's a nap schedule," Adelaide texted back.

Monday after school, on the court, Laurence lined up against Eddie for sprints. "Prepare to eat my dust," she said, and for once it wasn't a joke. She beat him by three steps, then five, and when Mr. Ngo blew the whistle for shooting drills, her legs felt like springs instead of sand. She hit nine free throws in a row.

"What did you do all weekend?" Eddie demanded.

"Nothing. That's the whole secret. Muscles get stronger after practice, not during it, so rest is part of getting better." She spun the ball on one finger. "Rest days. That's the plan now."

"So your training plan is napping."

"Elite napping," Laurence said, and sank another one from the top of the key.

activity: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
knowledge_domain: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
fact: French speakers normally address a server with the formal "vous," not the familiar "tu," which is kept for friends, family and children.
story:
The classroom smelled like burnt coffee from the teacher's lounge next door, and Ms. Visser had pushed the desks into little clusters with paper signs taped on top: Boulangerie, Café, Marché. Theo's sign said Restaurant Le Coq d'Or, and Taryn was his first customer, holding a laminated menu she had clearly decorated more than the assignment required.

"Bonjour," Theo began, his pronunciation still approximate at best. "Je voudrais... um... le poulet." He pointed at the menu so Taryn would know he meant the chicken and not some mystery dish. Then he wanted to ask the price, so he pushed on. "Combien... ça coûte?"

Taryn checked her cue card and said, "Dix euros," and Theo grinned so wide she laughed. "Tu es très bon serveur," he told her, pleased he remembered a compliment. Tye, at the next table over, made a choking sound into his sleeve.

"Wait, say that again," Tye said, wheeling his chair around. "The last part."

"Tu es très bon serveur?"

Tye shook his head slowly, like he was watching someone step on a rake. "Dude. You just talked to her like she's your little cousin. My mom does that all the time with my aunt, the tu thing, and once she said it to a hotel guy in Montreal and he got so stiff." Tye mimed a board straightening.

Theo looked at Taryn, who was still holding her menu. "But we say tu in every dialogue Ms. Visser gave us."

"Because we're all in the class together," Taryn said slowly. "We're like friends. But a server isn't. She's a stranger doing her job."

Theo sat with that. So the same word could be right in one mouth and wrong in another, depending on who was across the table. It was like how his dad wore one kind of shirt to a barbecue and another to a wedding, except this was baked into the grammar itself. He tested it in his head: Tye would get tu. Ms. Visser would get vous. His little cousin, tu. A waiter in an actual Paris café, and he felt a small cold drop of dread remembering the YouTube videos he'd watched last night where he'd confidently repeated every line, tu and all.

"That's why my app kept switching," he muttered. He'd assumed the app was being inconsistent. It hadn't been.

When it was Tye's turn to be the server, Theo raised his hand for another round. "Vous êtes très bon serveur," he said, laying the vous down like a card he'd been saving. Tye clutched his chest as if struck by elegance. "Combien ça coûte, s'il vous plaît?" The resentment Theo had been quietly nursing toward the whole French language, all those verbs that conjugated differently for no reason he could see, started to dissolve, because now he could see a reason.

"Gratuit," Tye announced grandly, "for a customer with manners."

Ms. Visser paused beside their table on her circuit of the room. "Un autre tour, Theo? You three have done four already."

"One more," Theo said. "I want to get it so smooth I don't have to think about it." He picked up his menu and straightened his imaginary apron. "Bonsoir, monsieur. Table pour deux?"

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: A voice deepens during puberty because the larynx grows and the vocal folds inside it get longer and thicker, and the voice may crack while this happens.
story:
Daniel stood in front of the pharmacy shelf labeled THROAT CARE and inhaled the sharp, medicinal smell of cough drops and menthol. He had a plan. His voice had cracked twice during the spring concert rehearsal, once so badly that Alyssa had turned around on the risers and stared at him, and he had decided, on the walk here, that a throat spray might fix whatever was going wrong. He picked up a blue bottle and read the back twice. "Soothes irritation," it said. His throat did not feel irritated. It felt like a stranger's throat.

Mr. Ma appeared beside him with a box of bandages he was restocking. "Looking for something specific?" Daniel held up the spray. "For my voice. It keeps breaking on the high notes." Mr. Ma tilted his head, the way he did when someone asked him for a medicine that did not exist. "You could try it," he said, and went back to his shelf, which was not exactly a recommendation.

Daniel bought the smallest bottle with his own money and tested it that evening on the back porch. He sprayed, waited, and sang the line from the concert that always betrayed him, the one that climbed toward the top of his range. Halfway up, his voice snapped in half like a dry twig, and somewhere across the fence a dog started barking. He tried again, slower. He tried lying down. He tried after drinking warm water. The crack moved around, sometimes on one note, sometimes on another, completely spontaneous, impossible to aim at or predict. Whatever was causing it, the spray was not reaching it.

That night he found a postcard from Felix, who had moved to a town almost at the equator, where Felix said it was too hot to think. "You're not going to believe what happened at my new school's choir," Felix had written. "A kid cracked so loud the whole bass section laughed, and then this other guy in my class, who reads medical books for fun, told me the actual reason. During puberty the larynx grows, and the vocal folds inside it get longer and thicker, and that's why the voice deepens. While it's growing, the voice can crack, because the folds haven't caught up yet. Nobody can spray their way out of it. It just has to finish growing. Sing low until then. See you in September, if I survive the heat."

Daniel read the postcard three times, then carried it up to his room and propped it against his lamp. He looked at his reflection in the dark window and hummed a low note, and it came out steady and deep, a sound he had never made before. When he tried the high note, it broke again, but this time he understood why, and somehow that made it almost interesting instead of humiliating. At the last rehearsal before the concert, Alyssa leaned over during the water break. "Still dying on the high part?" she asked. "No," Daniel said. "I'm just going to take the low harmony. It's growing." Alyssa frowned. "What is?" Daniel tapped his throat and grinned, and on the next song his new low note rolled out under everyone else's, round and strange and entirely his.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: According to the U.S. CDC, adults catch an average of two to three colds a year, and children often catch more.
story:
Sophia sat in the waiting room of the doctor's office with a tissue pressed to her nose, wondering whether it was even worth being there. She had counted on her fingers on the drive over: this was her third cold since fall started. Three. Her dad flipped through a magazine beside her, muttering about a story on hospital revenue, which seemed like a strange thing for a magazine to care about. "How can they guess that?" Sophia asked him, pointing at a number in the article. "It's an approximate figure," her dad said. "They estimate." Sophia thought about that word all the way to the exam room. An estimate. A guess built out of lots of real things.

She was still thinking about guessing when the door opened. Mr. Marino, her neighbor, shuffled in behind a nurse; he had the appointment after hers and had somehow wandered into the wrong room. "Third cold this winter," he announced to nobody in particular. "At my age, it's a disgrace." Sophia's ears went up. Third cold. He was a grown-up with three colds, and she was a kid with three colds, and suddenly she had a question she wanted answered more than she wanted her throat looked at.

When the nurse came back and started reading her chart, Sophia leaned forward. "Can I ask you something? Is three colds a lot?" The nurse smiled and said she'd send the doctor in, which was not an answer. Sophia kept thinking. If Mr. Marino had three and she had three, maybe three wasn't strange at all. Maybe it was an average, the way the magazine had an approximate number for revenue. But averages for who? Kids got sick more, didn't they? She tried to remember anyone she knew who never caught anything, and she couldn't. Even Fraser, who washed his hands like he was being paid to, had been sniffling before the holiday concert.

The doctor came in, listened to her lungs, and said it was a plain cold, rest and fluids. Sophia had one question left in her. "Is it weird that this is my third one since fall?" The doctor shook her head. "Adults average two to three colds a year, and kids often catch even more." Sophia blinked. Kids caught more than grown-ups. So Mr. Marino's three colds was about the top of normal for an adult, and her three was nothing unusual for someone her age at all.

On the drive home, she rolled the idea around. If catching colds was that ordinary, then the weird thing wasn't getting sick, it was Shawn's claim that he'd had one cold in two years. Either Shawn had a superpower, or Shawn was not counting the sniffles he called "allergies." She decided to test it. That afternoon she texted him: "Rate every snotty nose since September, one to ten, and tell me the dates." She sat cross-legged on her bed, waiting, a cup of tea going lukewarm beside her.

His reply came in three parts. First, "why." Then, "define snotty." Then, finally, a list with four items on it, including one he had labeled "just tired, nose ran a little." Sophia grinned and grabbed a pencil to modify his list, splitting the real colds from the fakes. So Shawn had three too, and he'd never noticed. She drew a box around the number and held the page up to the window.

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: Section 3 of the Canadian Charter gives every Canadian citizen the right to vote in elections for the House of Commons and provincial legislatures.
story:
Parker lay on the living room rug with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms spread open in front of him like a map he couldn't quite read. Mr. Morningstar had assigned each student one section to explain "in your own words, not the internet's words," and Parker had drawn Section 3, which was exactly three lines long and somehow still confusing. His cat, Boondoggle, sat on the corner of the page, accommodating himself on the paper as if it were furniture. "You're not helping," Parker told him, and Boondoggle blinked slowly, the way cats do when they know they're right.

The problem was the assignment itself. Explain a right in your own words. What did that even mean? He copied the words onto a sticky note and read them out loud to the ceiling. "Every citizen of Canada has the right to vote in an election of members of the House of Commons or of a legislative assembly." He said it twice more, slower, and then a piece clicked into place like a seatbelt. It said citizens. Not adults, not taxpayers, not people with jobs and income, just citizens. And it named the exact places you vote for: the House of Commons, and the provincial legislatures, which was the legislative assembly part. That was the whole fact, sitting right there. "Huh," he said, and Boondoggle's ears rotated toward him like tiny satellite dishes.

He grabbed his phone and texted Vihaan, who was doing the same assignment one street over.

Vihaan texted back a voice memo of himself groaning, then: "I got Section 3. It's the voting one, right? My mom votes, my dad votes, and I checked, even my great-aunt who lives in a cabin with no wifi votes. They all get to because they're citizens."

Parker sat up so fast the cat slid off the page. That was a test. If the rule was about citizenship, then it should cover Vihaan's whole family, wifi or no wifi, and it did. If the rule were about anything else, like age or income, his great-aunt might not fit, but she did fit. "Dude," Parker typed. "Your great-aunt just proved my theory."

"What theory? I sent you a fact about my aunt."

"I know. That's why it works."

Finnegan's little brother, who was seven, wandered over from next door because Finnegan's family was having a barbecue and the smell of burnt hot dogs had crossed the fence. He asked what Parker was doing, and Parker explained: "If you're a citizen of Canada, the Charter says you get to vote for the House of Commons, that's the federal one, or for your provincial legislature." The kid frowned. "Can I vote?" "You can when you're a citizen and old enough for the ballot, but the right in Section 3 is about being a citizen." The kid nodded as if this were the most normal conversation two people could have over a fence, and ran back to report to Finnegan that Parker was "doing homework outside on purpose, like a weirdo."

By Monday, Parker's paragraph was three sentences, all his own, and Mr. Morningstar read it twice. "This is probably the clearest one I've seen all day," he said. Parker grinned all the way back to his desk, and at lunch he told Vihaan that his great-aunt deserved partial credit. "Tell her she's famous," Vihaan said, stealing a fry. "Tell her she's evidence," Parker said, and stole it back.

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: Canada's census has let people report more than one ethnic or cultural origin since 1981, so the origin totals add up to more than the country's population.
story:
Hazel taped her poster to the wall of the art room and stood back to look at it, and her stomach dropped. The bar graph showed the ethnic and cultural origins of people in the town of Maple Creek, copied from census numbers, and beside each bar she had written a percentage. Scottish, 38 percent. Cree, 22 percent. Vietnamese, 14 percent. Ukrainian, 19 percent. She added them up on her calculator for the third time, and for the third time the answer came out to more than one hundred.

"You look like you're going to be sick," said Irene, who was arranging photos for her own project at the next table. The after-school heritage club met every Thursday, and today was the last day to finish posters for the display in the school hallway.

"My numbers don't work," Hazel said. "I checked the town website twice. The percentages add up to one hundred and thirty-two." Irene leaned over the graph and frowned at it, then shrugged.

Christopher wandered over with a glue stick in his hand. "Maybe the website made a mistake," he said. Hazel winced, because if the website was wrong then her whole poster was wrong, and she had spent two Thursdays on it.

Instead of arguing, she tried something. She grabbed a notebook and went around the room. "What origins do you put down for your family?" she asked Irene, then Christopher, then the two grade sevens building a family tree by the window. Irene said Jamaican and Irish. Christopher said Ukrainian and Métis. One grade seven said Chinese, Scottish, and Ojibwe. When Hazel counted, she had asked five people, but she had collected eleven origins.

She sat down slowly. "The people who filled out the census got to write down more than one," she said. "That's why the bars add up to more than everyone." She looked it up on the club's laptop to be sure, and there it was: the Canadian census had let people report more than one ethnic or cultural origin since 1981, so the origin totals added up to more than the country's population.

"So my poster isn't wrong," she said. "It just needed a sign." She wrote a note in marker and taped it under the title: "The bars add up to more than 100 percent because people can list more than one origin." Then she added a second sheet, sparse at first, just a heading: "Where our club comes from." By the end of the afternoon it was crowded with everyone's lists, including her own: Trinidadian, English, and, in her grandmother's handwriting, "proud artisan, potter, sixty years."

Ms. Bui came by with a roll of tape and read the poster twice. "The hallway display is going to start some good conversations," she said.

Hazel looked at her graph, at the bars that finally made sense, and said, "Maybe next time we survey the whole school."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: A Hanukkah menorah, or hanukkiah, has nine branches: eight for the eight nights of the holiday and one for the shamash, the helper candle used to light the others.
story:
The cultural center smelled like fried latkes and cardamom, and Nolan stood near the long table where three menorahs waited, their candles still unlit. His mother had volunteered to help set up the Hanukkah celebration this year, which was how Nolan ended up holding a box of candles while she arranged chairs to accommodate the crowd that would arrive within the hour. Alec had come along because his own parents were working late, and now he was squinting at the tallest menorah with his hands in his pockets.

"Okay, I have to ask," Alec said. "Hanukkah is eight nights, right? So why does that thing have nine spots for candles?"

Nolan opened his mouth to answer and then closed it again, because honestly he wasn't sure he could. He counted the branches with his finger, one through eight along the curve, and then the ninth one in the middle, standing taller than the rest. "Eight nights, eight candles," he said slowly. "And that one's different."

Last year at his grandmother's apartment, he remembered, she had always lit one candle first and used it to touch the others, one by one, while everyone sang. He had thought she was just being careful about matches. Now he turned the memory over like a puzzle piece. The tall middle candle never sat dark while the others burned; it always went first.

"Watch," Nolan said. He took a fresh candle, set it in the tall middle branch, and lit it with a match. Then he lowered its flame to the candle for the first night. "This one's called the shamash," he said. "The helper. It lights all the others, so the eight stay just for the eight nights."

Alec leaned in as the small flame caught. "Huh. So the nine together, but only eight count."

"Right." Nolan felt a small, bright flicker of getting it right, and then a quieter one behind it: his grandmother's hands doing this same thing last December, and the fact that she hadn't been well enough to travel this year. His mother waved him over to help stack napkins, and he gave the shamash one last look, still burning steady, doing its work while nobody called it one of the eight.

From the doorway, Mr. Zhao from the community office stuck his head in. "We're hanging the contemporary art banners in the east hall," he announced. "If anyone knocks over a candle, you're the defendant at my trial."

Alec laughed. Nolan carefully pinched out the match and dropped it in the cup of water by the table.

"Tallest candle, always first," Alec murmured, mostly to himself.

"That's the rule," Nolan said, and carried the box toward the kitchen.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: A stuffy nose during a cold is caused mainly by swollen blood vessels and inflamed tissue in the lining of the nose, not only by a buildup of mucus.
story:
Claire had blown her nose eleven times since breakfast, and the tissue box was down to its last four. Her nose still felt plugged, like someone had wedged a cork in it. The worst part was the timing: the school talent showcase was tonight at seven, and she had promised Raya and Eden she would run the soundboard while they performed.

She texted Eden. "Still sick. Nose won't unblock no matter what. Might miss tonight."

"Find something that works," Eden wrote back. "Raya says she can't follow the music cues without you."

Claire tried a hot shower, since her mom always suggested it. She stood under the steam for ten minutes and, for a little while, she could actually breathe. Then she dried off, walked back to her room, and the plug returned, as stubborn as before. She flopped on her bed and stared at the ceiling. If blowing removed mucus, and she'd blown out everything there was, why did the blockage stay? Something else had to be clogging the tunnel, something that wasn't mucus at all. She grabbed her phone and searched, typing fast.

The answer surprised her. She read it twice, then called Eden. "Guess what. A stuffy nose isn't mucus mostly. It's swollen blood vessels and inflamed tissue in the lining of the nose. That's what's blocking me. So blowing harder just makes it angrier."

"Okay, so what shrinks swelling?" Eden asked.

"Warmth, maybe. The shower worked for a bit." Claire checked the clock. Twelve forty. Seven hours. She could test it. She microwaved a damp washcloth, folded it, and pressed it over her nose and sinuses until it cooled. Breathe. Plugged. She microwaved it again, held it longer, then drank a big mug of warm soup broth, cupping her face over the steam. This time, when she tried breathing through her nose, air moved. Not a lot, but real air, and it stayed for nearly twenty minutes.

At five, Ms. Khoury knocked with a bag of lozenges from next door. "How's the patient?"

"Better. I'm going to comply with every rule my mom set, rest until six, then see if I can make it."

She did rest, flat on the couch, resisting the urge to do a vigorous test of her breathing every five minutes. At six thirty she stood, inhaled through her nose, and the air came through clear enough. She texted Raya: "On my way."

Raya replied with a single word, "Emperor!" which was their code for the best news possible. Claire grabbed her jacket and headed for the door.

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: On a distance-time graph, a flat horizontal line means the object is not moving.
story:
Isabella crouched at the top of the slide with a stopwatch in one hand and a tennis ball in the other, and below her Lincoln held a clipboard like it was a treasure map. "This is going to work," she said. "It has to work."

The assignment from Mr. Goh was simple to say and hard to do: measure the speed of a rolling ball using distance and time, then draw a distance-time graph. Speed was distance divided by time, which meant they needed both numbers, and they needed them for the same roll. They had chosen the playground because the rubber path near the swings was marked every metre with faded white paint. Perfect. Every two metres, Lincoln would call out the time, Isabella would write it down, and then they would extract the numbers from her notebook and turn them into a graph.

Jai stood halfway along the path with his phone, ready to film everything in case the stopwatch failed. "Hypothetical question," he said. "What if the ball stops halfway?"

"Then it stops halfway and we start over," Isabella said. She set the ball at the top of the little slope where the path began. "Three, two, one, go!"

She released the ball and Lincoln started the watch. "Two metres, two seconds! Four metres, four seconds!" The ball rolled straight and steady, and Isabella's pencil flew across the page. Then the ball drifted left, dropped off the path, and vanished into the hedge by the fence.

They all ran over. The ball was wedged deep in the branches, and Jai had to reach in with both arms to pull it out, while twigs snagged his sleeves. When he finally held it up, Isabella noticed the time on the stopwatch. It was still running. It read eleven seconds.

"Wait," she said, grabbing Lincoln's wrist. "When did it go into the hedge?"

"Right after the four-metre call," Lincoln said. "Maybe a second later. So it got stuck at about five metres."

Isabella sat down right there on the edge of the path and started the graph. She drew her axes, marked distance going up and time going across, and plotted the points. Two metres at two seconds. Four metres at four seconds. Then five metres at five seconds, and five metres at six seconds, and five metres at seven seconds, all the way to eleven seconds while they had been digging in the hedge.

She connected the dots and stared at it. The first part climbed like a ramp. Then something strange happened. The line went flat, straight across the page, not rising at all.

"It's flat," Lincoln said, leaning over her shoulder.

"That's where it was stuck," Isabella said, and her voice went up with excitement. "A flat line means it's not moving. The distance stays the same the whole time."

Jai crowded in to look. "So the graph tells the story by itself? Even the hedge part?"

"Even the hedge part." Isabella grinned and tapped the flat stretch with her pencil. "The ball sat in those branches for six whole seconds, and the line just goes sideways. Mr. Goh is going to love this."

She sprang up, brushed the dirt off her knees, and held the ball high. "One more run," she said, "and this time somebody guards the hedge."

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: A glow stick shines brighter but runs out faster when it is warm, and glows dimmer but lasts longer when it is cold.
story:
The car smelled like her mother's coffee and the fake pine air freshener that had been there since March. Kate turned the glow stick over in her fingers, watching its green light pulse faintly against her palm. "It's dimmer than it was," she said.

"It was in your warm pocket for an hour," her mother said, eyes on the road. "That one Adnan handed you was blazing bright when you got in."

Kate winced, remembering how Adnan had swung his stick around on the dance floor like a lighthouse, and how by the last song it had faded to almost nothing. He had laughed and tossed it in the bin on the way out. Her own stick, tucked in the pocket of her conventional grey jacket the whole evening, had never gotten that bright, but it was still going. She turned both ideas over in her head: his had been warm and brilliant and finished; hers had been warm-ish and modest and alive. There was a pattern there, but she couldn't see the cause of it, and that bothered her the way a loose thread bothers a sweater.

"Mom, do we have room in the freezer?"

"For a glow stick?"

"For a test." Kate held it up. "If warm makes them bright and quick, then cold might make them slow. I want to see if it's still glowing at breakfast."

Her mother glanced sideways, and Kate saw the look, the one that meant her mother was deciding whether to say something about how a first school dance usually ends with talk about the dance, not with science experiments. But her mother only said, "Move the peas. There's space behind the peas."

At home, Kate cracked the freezer door open slowly, so the cold rolled out over her wrist. She wedged the stick between a bag of peas and a box of fish sticks, where the light from it made a small green smear on the ice. She took a photo with her phone, in case her eyes played tricks on her overnight.

In the morning she was at the freezer before her toast. Behind the peas, the stick glowed, pale but definite, a thin green thread in all that frost. She carried it to the table still cold, holding it like evidence.

Her phone buzzed. Adnan: did your stick die yet? mine gave up at midnight lol.

She typed back a photo of the stick glowing against the frosty peas, then wrote, come over, I'll show you something. She set the stick on the windowsill in the sun and sat down to watch what happened next.

A few minutes later there was a knock, and Adnan came in with Maxence, holding a whole package of glow sticks from the gas station. "We're doing your experiment," Maxence said, "but this time with three. One cold, one warm, one in between." He put two in the freezer and set one on the sunny sill next to hers, and Kate pulled the peas aside to make room.

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: Card stacking is showing only the facts that support one side while leaving out the facts against it, so the message seems stronger than it is.
story:
Taylor had seventy-one dollars saved and a birthday coming, which meant the SpeedPro 9 tablet was almost, almost within reach. The ad filled her screen in a burst of music. "Everyone's switching," the screen announced, showing a line of laughing teenagers clutching identical tablets. A famous singer she recognized from Lyndon's playlists appeared next, holding one up. "The SpeedPro 9. Unbeatable. Revolutionary. The last tablet you'll ever need." Then came the list: five features, each with a glowing checkmark. Fastest processor. Sharpest screen. Lightest frame. Most storage. Coolest colors.

She leaned closer, then sat back, chewing her pen. Something about the list itched at her. Five great things, five checkmarks, and nothing else. She scrolled down, expecting more, and found only a Buy Now button.

She texted Vince, and ten minutes later he was on video call from his kitchen. "Look," she said, sharing her screen. "Everyone's switching, that's the bandwagon thing. The singer is a testimonial. And 'revolutionary' is just a loaded word. But look at the list."

"Five features," Vince said. "So?"

"So where's the battery life?" The question hung there. She opened a second tab and started hunting through reviews, though her signal kept dropping and the pages loaded in turbulent little freezes and jumps. Review after review scrolled past. Vince went quiet on his end.

She found it on the fourth review, written by a user named Marisol_88. "Battery dies in two hours," it said. Taylor read it aloud, slowly, feeling the ground tilt. Two hours. Every glowing checkmark on that ad was true, probably, but the ad only showed the facts that made the tablet look good and left out the ones against it, so the whole thing seemed stronger than it was.

"That's card stacking," Vince said, when she'd finished. "Ms. Paquette did a whole week on it last year. You stack the deck."

Taylor kept reading. Three more reviews mentioned the same problem, one from a person who said the company refused to distribute a software fix to customers who'd already paid. She closed the ad tab, and the music cut off mid-note, leaving her room silent except for the fan.

She opened her savings app instead and moved fifty dollars into a separate folder labeled RESEARCH. Then she typed a new search: SpeedPro 9 battery life complaint.

The first result was a forum thread with four hundred replies.

"Vince," she said, "you still got that tablet your cousin gave you?"

"Yeah, why?"

"How's the battery?"

He held it up to the camera, screen bright, and said, "Ask it yourself."

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: Emergency agencies advise unplugging computers and other electronics during a power cut, because a surge of electricity when the power returns can damage them.
story:
The lights went out at 8:14, right in the middle of Victoria's history essay. She sat in the dark kitchen listening to the refrigerator die, then grabbed her phone and called Melody.

"Transformer blew, probably," Melody said from three streets over, where her lights were also out. "My dad says the crew can't get here before ten."

Victoria clicked her phone off to save the battery and felt her way to the junk drawer for the big flashlight. Its beam swung across the living room, and she stopped. The desktop computer sat dark on its desk, still plugged in. The gaming console glowed with its little orange standby light, drinking power that no longer existed.

Here was the problem. When the crew fixed the transformer at ten, all that electricity would come rushing back at once, and her mom had said once, half-asleep on the couch, that a surge like that could fry anything still plugged in. That computer held her essay, half her photos, and every save file she cared about. The console was durable, but not that durable. The logic was simple: no plug, no surge. She went around the room like a detective, yanking cords. The lamp, the microwave, the TV. She texted Bruno to do the same, and he sent back a photo of himself tripping over his own charging cable, which made her laugh out loud alone in the dark.

Then she found the modem blinking its battery-powered lights in the hallway, and she stopped. If she unplugged it, the battery backup died too, and when the power came back, everything would have to restart from scratch. If she left it, the surge might take it out and they'd be without internet for days. "Come on, think," she told the flashlight. Her dad needed the internet for work in the morning. She pulled that plug too.

She still had two hours to kill by flashlight, so she lit the emergency candle, spread her history notes on the kitchen table, and wrote her essay by hand, slower than typing but somehow better sentences. At 9:51 the lights blazed back on and the refrigerator accelerate... no, it coughed and hummed and came back to life like an old man getting up from a chair. Every screen in the house stayed dark, safe and silent.

Her mom came home at 9:58 and stood in the bright doorway holding takeout. "Why is everything unplugged?"

"Surge," Victoria said. "Ask the flashlight. Also, my essay exists on paper now, in cursive, like a pioneer."

Her mom held up the takeout bag. "Cold noodles, since the microwave's dead too."

"I unplugged it for its own good, Mom."

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons, so the atomic number also tells you how many electrons it has.
story:
Jace spread the science project across the kitchen table like a detective laying out evidence. The assignment was due tomorrow: draw a model of a sodium atom, label the particles, and show his work. He had the paper, the colored pencils, and a printout of the periodic table. The only problem was that the paper was blank, because he had no idea how many electrons to draw.

He called Nahla, who lived two floors up in the same building.

"How many electrons did you draw for yours?" he asked the moment she picked up.

"I'm not telling you the answer," Nahla said. "Mr. Girma would know. But I'll come down and sit with you while you figure it out. Ten minutes."

She arrived with her own binder and a granola bar, which she broke in half and pushed the bigger piece across the table to him, because she knew he always forgot to eat when he was stuck. She settled into the chair their tenant usually sat in on Sunday mornings and waited.

Jace dragged his finger across the printout. "Okay. Sodium. Atomic number eleven. So that means eleven protons, I got that part. But electrons?" He squinted at the tiny square as if it might whisper the answer. It looked faintly sinister, sitting there in its little box, keeping its secret.

"Draw what you do know," Nahla suggested. "Start with the protons in the middle."

He drew a cluster of eleven small plus signs in a nucleus, then sat back. "A neutral atom," he said slowly, reading off the top of his notes, where Mr. Girma had written it on the board and underlined it twice. "Neutral. Not positive, not negative." He tapped his pencil against the table. "If the protons make it positive, and electrons make it negative, and the whole thing is neutral..."

Nahla reached over and stole one of his blue pencils to start her own drawing, just so he wouldn't feel watched.

"Then they have to cancel out," Jace said. "Eleven protons means eleven electrons. In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons. So the atomic number gives you both."

He allocated the electrons to their shells the way the textbook diagram showed, two in the first ring, eight in the second, one lonely electron spinning in the outermost orbit. He labeled it carefully, then checked sodium's square one more time. Eleven. Protons, eleven. Electrons, eleven. It balanced.

There was a knock at the door. Mr. Girma from down the hall stood there holding a plate of cookies. "I heard pencils moving through the wall," he said, peering past Jace at the drawing. "Is that sodium?"

Jace held it up. "Eleven protons, eleven electrons, neutral atom."

Mr. Girma smiled and set the plate on the table next to the half granola bar. "I'll leave you two to it, then. Save me a cookie."

Nahla was already copying the diagram into her own binder, her pencil moving fast. "Jace," she said without looking up, "check nitrogen for me. Number seven?"

Jace ran his finger down the column, found it, and picked up a fresh cookie.

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: The Sieve of Eratosthenes, an ancient Greek method, lists primes by crossing out the multiples of each prime in turn.
story:
The clock on Cristian's basement wall said 6:40, and the coding club showcase started at 7:30, which meant Kaitlyn had fifty minutes to make her program stop lying. She had written a Python program that asked for a number and printed whether it was prime, and it worked fine for 7 and 11, but when she typed 9, it proudly announced PRIME.

"That's wrong," Cristian said, leaning over her shoulder with a soda radiating cold against her arm. "Nine is three times three."

"I know what nine is," Kaitlyn said, but her cheeks went hot anyway. Karim was sprawled on the couch with a marker and a big sheet of graph paper, drawing a grid of numbers from 2 to 50 for the club's poster. "I checked every number by dividing by two. If it doesn't divide by two, it's prime, right?"

Karim snorted without looking up. "Fifteen doesn't divide by two."

Kaitlyn stared at the screen. Fifteen. Three times five. Her whole method was built on one test, and one test could not cover everything. She needed to divide by more numbers, but which ones, and how far? She tried dividing by every number up to n, and that worked, but for 47 it took forever, and the showcase needed the program to answer fast while people watched.

"Wait," she said slowly. "Karim, what are you doing to that grid?"

"Crossing out multiples," Karim said. "Two, so four, six, eight, all gone. Then three, so six, nine, twelve. Then five. It's called the Sieve of Eratosthenes, some old Greek thing. Ms. Shapiro showed us." He circled 2, then 3, then 5, then 7, and pointed at the survivors scattered across the paper like islands. "Whatever's left is prime."

Kaitlyn grabbed the sheet and pulled it close. Every number crossed out was a multiple of some smaller number, and every number still circled was immune to being crossed out, because no smaller prime divided it. And here was the part that made her bounce in her chair: by the time Karim reached 7, the next unmarked number after it, 49, was seven sevens, and everything smaller than 49 that wasn't prime had already been crossed out by 2, 3, or 5. She did not need to test every divisor. She only needed the primes up to the square root of n.

She typed fast, deleting her old loop and writing a new one that divided only by small numbers and stopped early. Cristian read the line out loud as she finished it, and Karim abandoned the poster to watch.

"Try nine," Cristian said, like a game show host.

She typed 9. NOT PRIME. She typed 25. NOT PRIME. She typed 97, held her breath, and the screen said PRIME so fast it felt like an echo. Karim checked it against his grid, where 97 would have sat far past the last row, uncrossed if he ever extended the paper.

"Forty-seven's still prime?" Cristian asked.

"Forty-seven has always been prime," Kaitlyn said. "My program just didn't know it yet." She saved the file twice, closed the laptop halfway like it was something breakable, and pointed at the stairs. "Grab the poster. We have twenty minutes."

Karim rolled the grid into a tube. "The Sieve of Eratosthenes, ladies and gentlemen."

"Move," Kaitlyn said, already three steps up.

activity: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
knowledge_domain: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
fact: Resistance is measured in ohms, written with the Greek letter omega.
story:
Hannah crouched on the garage floor next to Ms. Chen's workbench, holding a coil of copper wire in both hands like it might bolt for the door. She needed a science project that would actually work this time, not another baking-soda volcano that fizzled out in front of everyone. "So I measure the voltage across the wire, then the current through it," she said slowly, reading from her notebook, "and the resistance is the ratio of one to the other."

"That's the plan," Ms. Chen said. She clipped the wire into the circuit and spun the dial on her multimeter. "Tell me what the screen shows."

Hannah leaned in. The number was 4.7, and beside it sat a strange symbol, a looping shape like a horseshoe standing on end. "Four point seven horseshoes?" she said. Everett, who was sprawled on an old lawn chair recording data, snorted so hard he nearly dropped the pencil.

"It's not a horseshoe," Ms. Chen said, smiling. "That's omega, the Greek letter. Resistance is measured in ohms, written with the Greek letter omega." Hannah wrote it down, drawing the loop twice until it looked right. It reminded her of last spring, when she had stood at the whiteboard convinced her answer was correct because it "felt" right, and Ms. Chen had said that science was not about feelings, because feelings were subjective and the universe did not care what felt true. Hannah had flushed to her ears that day. Now she measured things twice.

"Okay," she said. "So if the resistance is voltage divided by current, and I change the voltage, the resistance should stay the same, because it's a property of the wire. If my numbers violate that, I did something wrong." Everett sat up straighter. "Wait, that's actually a test? Like the wire can't lie?" "That's exactly what it is," Hannah said, and her heart beat a little faster.

They ran the experiment five times. At 3.0 volts and 0.31 amps, then 6.0 volts and 0.62 amps, then 9.0 and 0.93, the division came out to almost the same number every single time. Hannah checked each result on her calculator while Everett read the meter aloud, and Ms. Chen watched from her stool without saying a word. On the fifth run the answer jumped to 40, and Hannah frowned at the clips before realizing one had slipped loose and was touching the paint of a coffee can. She fixed it, reran it, and got 9.9.

"Ten ohms," Everett said, pointing at the little omega on the screen. "Give or take." Hannah copied the number into her notebook, drew the symbol one more time, and then held the wire up to the garage light, turning it slowly. "You were hiding this the whole time," she told it. Everett laughed and clicked the pen closed.

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: Teasing often depends on an audience, so walking away with the targeted classmate, saying something like "Come on, let's go," can end it without a confrontation.
story:
Jordan had discovered the trick by accident at his cousin's birthday party the summer before. A kid named Tomas was getting grilled about his stutter, a circle of boys leaning in like it was a show, and Jordan had simply grabbed his sleeve and said they needed help carrying the snacks. The circle broke apart the second the two of them walked into the kitchen. Nobody had to be brave in that hallway. The audience had just left.

Now it was October, and Blaine was the one in the circle. It had started near the lockers before science, Vladimir doing most of the talking, a small crowd doing the laughing. Blaine's science folder had slid open and his volcano diagram, the one with the monsoon of red marker arrow labeled "lava flow" pointed the wrong direction, was being held up like evidence in a trial.

"Even the volcano's ashamed of it," Vladimir said, and the crowd supplied the laughter again, right on cue.

Jordan stood there holding his own folder and thought about the party. The problem, as far as he could figure it, wasn't really Vladimir. Vladimir had been mediocre at best before eighth grade, but he'd learned that teasing Blaine worked, and it worked because the crowd kept showing up. Take the crowd away and the whole thing might just deflate, the way it had in that kitchen with Tomas. Jordan wasn't sure. It was a theory, and like Mr. Zhou kept saying about their lab experiments, you didn't know until you ran it.

He crossed the hall. "Blaine, come on, let's go," he said, nodding toward Mr. Zhou's door. "Mr. Zhou said he wanted help setting up the erosion demo before class."

Blaine blinked at him. "He did?"

"He did," Jordan said, with what he hoped would convey certainty rather than total invention. Blaine glanced once at the diagram still in Vladimir's hand, then let it drop to the floor and followed.

Jordan kept talking about the erosion demo, inventing details about sand trays and a spray bottle, and by the time they reached the classroom doorway he looked back. The circle had come apart into two kids checking phones and one wandering off. Vladimir was left standing there holding Blaine's volcano diagram with nobody to show it to, which was its own kind of punishment.

Inside, Mr. Zhou was stacking sand trays, and it turned out he actually did need help with the erosion demo. He handed them a spray bottle and asked where they'd been. Blaine opened his mouth, then looked at Jordan.

"We were helping carry stuff," Jordan said.

Mr. Zhou looked at the two of them for a moment longer than necessary, then at the spray bottle. "Start with the slope at thirty degrees," he said. "And, Jordan, next time you invent an errand, pick one I haven't already assigned you."

Blaine snorted. Jordan picked up the sand tray.

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: The equals sign was invented by the Welsh mathematician Robert Recorde in 1557, who chose two parallel lines because no two things could be more equal.
story:
Hazel slid her practice sheet across the library table and frowned at the first problem: x + 7 = 19. Tomorrow was the makeup quiz, and if she failed it, she would be benched for Saturday's track meet. Kyrie had already aced his test, and Zachery claimed the equations were easy, which made it worse.

"You take the seven off the left," Kyrie said, tapping the paper, "but you have to take it off both sides. Same move, both sides."

"Why both?" Hazel asked. "The seven is only on one side." She looked up at the shelves behind them, where Mr. Popescu was pushing a cart of returns. The library smelled like pencil shavings and old paper, and the radiator under the window ticked as it cooled.

Mr. Popescu set down a book called Mathematicians: A Memoir of the Great Minds and let it fall open near their table. "Look who drew that," he said, pointing at a page, and walked away before Hazel could ask him anything. She leaned over. There was a picture to illustrate the old notation, the strangest equals sign she had ever seen, long and slanted. "Listen to this," she said slowly. "The equals sign was invented by the Welsh mathematician Robert Recorde in 1557. He chose two parallel lines because no two things could be more equal." She ran her finger under the printed line, reading it twice to be sure she had it right.

"Parallel," Zachery said, "like train tracks. Never touching, always the same distance apart." Hazel stared at the sign in her own equation. Two sides. The same, all the way down. She tried a small experiment, something she could test: she took x + 7 = 19 and subtracted seven from the left only. She got x = 19 on one side and a lopsided 12 on the other, which could not be right, because if the sides were equal before, they had to stay equal after. So she subtracted seven from both sides instead. x = 12. She checked it: 12 plus 7 was 19. It balanced, like the two parallel lines, like a scale with a weight on each pan.

Her pencil moved faster down the sheet. She tried 3x = 15 and divided both sides by three, and then 5x minus 4 = 26, adding four to both sides before dividing by five. Each answer fit when she checked it, every single one. Zachery flipped a page of the memoir and found a picture of Recorde's actual book, the slanted lines printed there in ink gone brown with age. "This guy invented a symbol the whole world still uses," he said.

Hazel wrote one more equation at the bottom of her page, x minus 3 = 9, then drew a careful equals sign, two straight parallel lines, and whispered, "No two things could be more equal." She picked up her pencil and solved it in a single clean line.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: In a 1974 study by Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer, people who were asked how fast cars 'smashed' into each other gave higher speed estimates than people asked about cars that 'hit.'
story:
The message popped up at 9:14, right after James finished his math homework: "EMERGENCY. Did anyone see what happened in the east hallway after last period?" Thalia had sent it in all caps, which meant trouble. Mathieu answered first. "I saw it. Marcus and that kid from Mr. Barrett's class slammed into each other going full speed." James typed back that he'd been near the water fountain, maybe ten meters away, and it hadn't looked that fast to him. Marcus was limping, sure, but people bumped in that hallway every day.

Thalia's next message arrived in pieces, the way she typed when she was worked up. "My mom asked me how fast they were going when they smashed into each other. She thinks the other kid should be suspended. She's going to email the school tomorrow." James stared at the screen. Something about the word "smashed" bothered him, like a stone in his shoe. He remembered the sound, and it had been more of a thud.

"I'm going to verify this," he typed. "What exactly did your mom ask you?" He waited, thumbs hovering. Mathieu sent a shrug emoji. Thalia replied, "She asked how fast they were going when they smashed into each other. Why?" James didn't answer right away. Instead he opened a search page and typed: do the words people use change how you remember something?

He found it within a minute, on a page about memory research. In 1974, Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer had run a study. People who were asked how fast cars smashed into each other gave higher speed estimates than people who were asked how fast cars hit each other. Same films. Different verb. James read it twice, then a third time, his door rattling as his sister laid siege to it wanting the charger. "Not now," he called.

He copied the sentence and pasted it into the chat. "So here's the thing," he typed. "Nobody actually knows how fast they were going. Thalia, your mom asked you with the word smashed. Mathieu, you said full speed. I said bump. And we all saw the same hallway." The typing bubble appeared under Thalia's name, vanished, appeared again. She was hesitant; James could almost see her chewing her lip.

"Okay," she finally sent. "But my mom already wrote the email. It's in her drafts." James called her, holding the phone to his ear while he paced. "Tell her to reread her own question," he said. "Then tell her what Mathieu said when nobody used that word yet." There was a pause on the line, then Thalia's voice went muffled, and he heard her say, "Mom? Before you send that, can I ask you something about how you asked me?"

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: In a healthy onion cell, the cell membrane is pressed tightly against the inside of the cell wall, which makes the membrane very hard to see as a separate line.
story:
Paisley sat in the waiting room of the animal clinic with her cat carrier on her knees and her science homework balanced on top of it. The sheet said to draw an onion cell and label the cell wall, the cell membrane, and the nucleus. She had the wall, easy, a thick brick-colored outline. She had the nucleus, a dark dot like a swallowed peppercorn. But the membrane was nowhere. She had redrawn the same cell four times.

"That's a microscope, isn't it?" Rayyan said, pointing through the doorway into the back room, where a squat gray machine sat on a counter between shelves of sample jars. Rayyan was there with his gecko, Reginald, who had stopped eating crickets. What Rayyan wanted, mostly, was to see that microscope up close, and possibly to look at something disgusting through it.

"My grandma's cat needs his teeth checked," Zaiden said from the next chair. "I'm the lucky escort." He leaned over Paisley's drawing. "Why is there an arrow pointing at nothing?"

"That's the problem. The membrane's supposed to be there and it isn't. Maybe onion cells don't have one."

Mr. Adebayo came out with a clipboard, and when Paisley's mother explained that their old cat, Muffin, was being seen for drinking too much water, he nodded and said it would be a few minutes. Paisley asked, in a rush, whether the clinic's microscope might be free.

He looked at her worksheet, then at the clock, and said they had time between patients, but she had to be careful and not dismantle anything. She carried the slide like it was a soap bubble. In the back room, on a counter beside a jar labeled only anonymous, she set the onion skin under the lens and squinted. Wall. Nucleus. Between the wall and the inside, nothing but a clean empty gap where the line should be.

Rayyan had his face practically on her shoulder. "Told you. No membrane."

"Everything alive has a membrane," Zaiden said. "We learned that. It's like the skin under the shell. It has to be there."

Paisley stared at the flat gray bricks of the cells. Then she thought about the one thing she knew: the membrane had to be pressed right up against the inside of the wall. She traced the wall's inner edge with her pencil, pressing hard, then lifted the pencil and looked. The wall now looked like two lines, a thick one and a thin one, tight together. "It's not missing," she said slowly. "It's hidden. It's squeezed against the wall so you can't see it as a separate line unless you know where to look." She drew both lines and labeled the thin one, her hand steady.

Mr. Adebayo looked in from the doorway. "Nice work. Muffin's ready now, and I'll be honest, we need to run more tests."

Paisley carried her finished drawing back to the waiting room, and behind her Rayyan was already asking, "So what's the ratio of weird stuff you could look at under that thing? Like, ear wax?"

Paisley sat down next to the carrier and slid her finger through the mesh door. Muffin blinked at her, slow and yellow-eyed.

"Tomorrow we'll know more," her mother said.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: In the Dutch Republic, prices for rare tulip bulbs soared in the winter of 1636 to 1637 and then collapsed in February 1637, when buyers stopped showing up.
story:
The last box of Frost-Cola cereal sat alone on the top shelf, and the price tag beneath it made Lincoln stop so fast his sneakers squeaked on the floor. Six dollars. Last month the same box had cost three. He looked down the aisle at the pyramid of plain oat cereal, stacked to his shoulder, marked two for five dollars. Something was going on here that he could not see, some rule working behind the prices like gears inside a clock.

He found his mother by the strawberries, which were piled in red heaps and selling cheap, and beside her stood Gurshan with his own cart. Gurshan held his phone out. "You see this?" On the screen was a marketplace post offering a Strato-Dragon card for eighty dollars. "Same card I traded you my extra for in December. Everyone wants one. There are only like ten in the whole school."

Lincoln took the phone and studied the post, the smell of strawberries sweet and cold in his nose. He remembered the poster in Ms. Visser's classroom, the one about the Dutch Republic, and the line he had copied into his notebook because it sounded impossible. "In the winter of 1636 to 1637, rare tulip bulbs in the Dutch Republic cost more than people could believe," he said slowly. "Then in February 1637 the prices collapsed. Buyers just stopped showing up." Gurshan stared at him. "So the same thing could happen to the Strato-Dragon." Lincoln nodded. "Cheap thing, lots of it. Rare thing, everybody wants it. Then the wanting stops, and the price falls off a cliff."

They decided to demonstrate the idea right there in the store. Gurshan became the buyer, Lincoln the seller, and the two forlorn bottles of spicy mango soda on the endcap became the rare bulbs. "Five dollars each," Lincoln announced, holding them up. Gurshan, playing an obstinate shopper, shook his head and bargained down to four, and a woman reaching past them for orange juice laughed. Then Gurshan wheeled his cart into the juice aisle, where gallons stood in crowded rows, and offered Lincoln one dollar for the next bottle Lincoln touched. Nobody wanted what was everywhere. The pattern held. It held all the way to the registers, where a man ahead of them paid nine dollars for the second-to-last bag of storm-tracked ice melt, and the cashier said, "Rain's coming, everybody wants it."

At school the next morning Gurshan grabbed Lincoln's sleeve before first period. His face was pale. "The Strato-Dragon. Lily-Rose found out there are two hundred of them. Somebody opened a whole case from the mall this weekend. They're not rare at all." Down the hall, Lily-Rose was already waving a Strato-Dragon in the air like a flag, and behind her came a boy Lincoln had never traded with before, holding out a card and saying, "Eighty dollars. Take it or leave it, but I need the money today."

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: Shirley Jackson's story The Lottery, published in The New Yorker in 1948, opens with children piling up stones, a detail that hints at how the lottery ends.
story:
Mya arrived at book club carrying her copy of the story flat against her chest, like a shield, because she had not finished it. She had read to the middle on the bus and then fallen asleep, and now Syeda and Magalie were already arguing about the ending at the little table by the library window.

"You're biased," Syeda said, "because you guessed wrong." Magalie had guessed the lottery would be for a prize, which, to be fair, was a reasonable thing to guess.

Mr. Baptiste held up his hand. "Before anyone spoils anything further, we have a member who hasn't finished. Mya, go read the last three pages in the corner. We'll wait. We'll be quiet, which will be hard."

It was hard. Mya read the ending with her back to them, and when she turned around her face apparently said everything, because Syeda pointed at her and said, "See."

"Okay," said Mr. Baptiste. "Now the real work. Reread the first paragraph. The very first one, the calm one, from The New Yorker, 1948. What does Jackson put there?" He would not say more. He had this policy of standing by the window and drinking his terrible coffee while they floundered, and he seemed to enjoy it.

The paragraph was full of sunshine, grass, flowers, boys running around gathering stones. Mya read it twice. On the bus it had seemed like set dressing, the literary equivalent of a welcome mat. Now it sat there like a loaded water pistol in a cheerful family photo. She assessed it line by line, the way she'd been taught, hunting for anything that didn't belong at a picnic.

"The stones," she said slowly. "The kids are piling them up in the corner. Nobody explains why. And the whole story goes by and nobody explains why, until..." She stopped, not wanting to say the ending out loud, as if it could still be un-happened.

"Until the lottery," Magalie finished.

"It was there the whole time," Mya said. "Page one. First paragraph. She basically told us, and I read right past it." She felt like a scavenger who had walked over buried meat all afternoon and then complained there was nothing to eat. "So that's foreshadowing. And the stones aren't just stones. They mean the whole tradition, probably. Something old and ordinary and awful."

"Write that down," said Mr. Baptiste, "before you get shy about it."

Mya wrote it in the margin of her copy, in pencil, small. Syeda leaned over to read it, then flipped to the first page and read the paragraph a third time with narrowed eyes.

"Children," Syeda said. "Piling up stones. On a sunny day." She looked up. "I'm never trusting a sunny day again."

"Reasonable," said Mya, and turned the page back to the ending.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: Antibiotics kill bacteria but have no effect on viruses, so they do not help cure a cold or the flu.
story:
Zoey stood in the aisle of the pharmacy on Willow Street, holding a box of tissues and staring at a shelf of cough syrup like it might stare back. She had been home with the flu for four days, and tomorrow was the tryout for the spring play, the one Hazel had promised they would audition for together since November. If she missed it, there would be no other chance.

"Mom, can we just ask the pharmacist for the strong stuff?" Zoey whispered. Her mother was comparing two bottles of fever reducer, and behind them a boy about Zoey's age leaned on the counter, talking to Mr. Nikolaidis, the pharmacist who also lived on their street.

"My doctor won't give me antibiotics," the boy was saying. "I have a soccer game Saturday. I need to be better by then."

Mr. Nikolaidis tapped the counter. "You can't rush this one with antibiotics. Antibiotics kill bacteria, but they have no effect on viruses. A cold or the flu is a virus, so they won't help cure it."

Zoey turned the box of tissues over in her hands. So that was why the doctor had just told her mother to wait it out. She had been thinking of the flu like a splinter, something you could pull out if you found the right tool. It was more like a storm; you could only hold on until it passed.

"Then what does work?" the boy asked.

"Rest, fluids, time," Mr. Nikolaidis said. "Boring, but true."

Zoey stepped up to the counter. "Mr. Nikolaidis? If I've been resting for four days, is that enough time? I have a tryout tomorrow."

He looked at her over the rim of his glasses, as if adjusting a lens to bring her into focus. "How's the fever?"

"Gone since this morning."

"Then your body's winning. You might not feel lush and green tomorrow, but you'll be standing."

On the drive home, Zoey texted Hazel: Can you ask if I can audition last, like at the end? Might give me a few more hours.

Hazel replied with a row of exclamation marks. Already did. You're slotted after me. Rest, weirdo.

Zoey slept until dinner, woke to soup, and slept again. In the morning her throat was still scratchy and her legs felt like they wanted to hibernate through another week, but her head was clear. Hazel met her at the auditorium door and pressed a bottle of water into her hand.

"Your voice sounds like a rusty gate," Hazel said.

"Perfect for the villain," Zoey said, and walked toward the stage.

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: Shaking a baby can cause serious brain injury, because an infant's neck muscles are too weak to support its heavy head.
story:
The note on the fridge said everything Avery needed: feed at seven, crib is in the corner room, call if anything seems wrong, back by ten. Mrs. Okafor had paused at the door with the diaper bag over her shoulder and said, "Do you want me to clarify anything before I go?" Avery had almost said no, just to sound confident, but instead she asked about the bottle warming and the nap schedule, and she was glad she did, because the answers mattered.

The baby, a chubby three-month-old named Pip, stared up at her from the blanket on the floor like she was the most interesting thing that had ever happened. For the first hour, everything was easy. Pip chewed her fist, kicked her legs, and let out small delighted hoots whenever Avery made a face. Avery texted Mahee: This is the best job ever. Fifteen dollars for playing with a baby. Mahee texted back: The median babysitting rate in our town is probably twelve, you're rich.

Then, at eight o'clock, Pip started to cry. Not the polite fussing from before, but a red-faced, air-raid siren wail that went on and on. Avery walked her, bounced her, sang a song she made up on the spot, checked the diaper, offered the bottle again. Nothing worked. Her arms ached and her ears rang, and a hot, frantic feeling climbed up her neck.

Her phone buzzed. Mahee again: lol just shake her till she stops. Avery's stomach dropped. No, she typed back fast. Never. My babysitting class said shaking a baby can seriously injure her brain. Their neck muscles are too weak to hold up a heavy head. Mahee replied with a horrified face and "I WAS KIDDING," but Avery was already moving. She laid Pip gently on her back in the crib, made sure the blanket was loose and away from her face, and stepped out to the hallway to breathe. Five minutes, the instructor had said. The baby is safe in the crib. You can take five minutes. That was the rule, and now it made complete sense.

From the hallway, she heard something through the baby monitor that made her freeze. The crying wasn't steady at all. It came in waves, and right before each wave, there was a tiny clicking sound. She crept back to the doorway and watched. Pip's face was scrunched, her knees pulling up to her belly, and her fists were clenched tight. Avery had read a page about this, and suddenly the pieces snapped together. Gas. Tummy trouble. It wasn't her fault, and it wasn't random.

She remembered the dryer humming in the laundry room, a low warm rumble, and the way Mrs. Okafor had mentioned Pip sometimes calmed with noise and motion.
