Avery scooped her up carefully, supporting that heavy head with her whole hand, and carried her into the laundry room. She flipped the empty dryer on and swayed. The machine thumped and rolled behind them, vibrating faintly through the floorboards, and the smell of clean towels hung in the warm air.

Pip gave one last hiccupping wail, then a shudder, then went quiet. Her eyes drifted shut mid-cry, like the nap had been completely spontaneous, and Avery stood there in the humming dark feeling like she had solved a mystery worthy of a whole detective agency.

At ten, Mrs. Okafor came through the door and tiptoed over to peek at the crib. "She's asleep? After her fussy evening?" Then she looked at the running dryer and laughed softly. "You found it. Her dad does the same trick." Avery grinned all the way to the kitchen, where her fifteen dollars waited on the counter, and Mahee's next text was already lighting up her phone: TELL ME EVERYTHING.

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: On a distance-time graph, a line that curves upward and gets steeper shows an object speeding up.
story:
Felix set the meter stick across two stacks of books and propped one end on Grayson's binder, making a ramp that leaned like a frail cardboard hill. "Ms. Ricci said we measure distance and time, then draw the graph ourselves," he said. "I want the steepest ramp in the class."

"That's a mistake," Grayson said. "A steep ramp means the ball goes fast the whole way, so the graph will just be one straight line, up like a wall. You should oppose my idea if you want, but I'm telling you, straight ramp, straight line."

Charles-Etienne was timing with the stopwatch app on his phone, and Felix had taped a long paper strip along the floor marked every twenty centimeters. "We call out each mark as the ball passes it," Felix said. "Charles-Etienne writes down the time. Then we plot it." He glanced at the wall poster of a deer labeled HERBIVORE: EATS ONLY PLANTS, which had nothing to do with physics but made the lab feel like the lab.

They released the marble. "Twenty!" called Felix. "Forty!" Charles-Etienne's thumb hammered the lap button. "Sixty! Eighty!" When they plotted the points, Felix drew the line through them and frowned. It was not straight. It began almost flat, then bent upward, growing steeper and steeper toward the end, like a slide that scooped down.

"Your graph is wrong," Grayson said. "You missed a mark." They ran it again, and then a third time, and each graph came out the same shape, curving up, getting steeper. Felix tapped the paper. "The line starts shallow because the ball is slow at the top. It ends steep because the ball is going fastest at the bottom. The curve means it's speeding up the whole way down." He ran his finger along the bending line. "A steeper part is a faster moment."

Grayson leaned over the points for a long moment, then set down his pencil. "I change my mind," he said quietly. "I wanted a straight line because it was easier to draw. But the curve is better. It tells more."

That evening Felix wrote a note to leave on Grayson's desk before class.

"Grayson, I looked at our three graphs again. Every one curves upward, steeper at the end, even though we dropped the ball from different heights each time. It's never a straight line when the ball speeds up. Tomorrow I want to try a flat track on the floor, because I think that one won't curve. If I'm right, the flat-track graph will prove the ramp graph. Your friend, Felix."

The next morning Grayson was already at the lab bench, the ramp rebuilt, the paper strip smoothed flat, two stopwatches lined up beside the marble. He looked up when Felix came in. "I borrowed a second stopwatch from Ms. Ricci," he said, "so we can check each other's times." He rolled the marble down the ramp one more time, and both of them watched it fly off the end and across the floor.

activity: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll
knowledge_domain: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll
fact: When defenders switch on a pick and roll, it can create a mismatch, such as a tall player guarding a quick guard or a short player guarding a tall one.
story:
Levi stood at the top of the driveway with the ball on his hip, counting the cones Ms. Virtanen had set out as pretend defenders. Brodie planted himself beside cone three, ready to screen.

"Call something," Brodie said. "You're the point guard. Point guards talk."

Levi knew the words. He had watched his cousin run a pick and roll a hundred times on TV, and he could picture it: Brodie would step out and block Levi's defender, Levi would dribble past, and then Brodie would roll to the basket. The problem was calling it out loud. His voice had a way of disappearing when other kids were listening, and today Asees was watching from the porch steps, arms crossed, waiting to be impressed or disappointed.

"Pick and roll," Levi finally said, too quiet.

"What?"

"Pick and roll!" He pointed at Brodie, then at the rim, drawing two parallel lines in the air like the two paths they would take, side by side and then splitting apart.

Brodie jogged over and set the screen. Levi rubbed off it, and Asees, playing defense from the porch, jumped out to cut him off. Levi spun and found Brodie rolling hard to the hoop, but Asees's little sister had wandered onto the court, and everyone froze so nobody plowed her over.

"That's a switch," Asees said, walking the girl back to the sandbox like a mother marsupial carrying its young. "I picked up Brodie now. You got the little kid's spot." She grinned, because Brodie was a head taller than her, and she looked tiny beside him.

Levi's first thought was that the play was ruined. His second thought was the interesting one. Asees was quick, the quickest defender out here, and she was guarding the tallest player on the driveway. That did not seem like a problem for the defense. It seemed like a problem Asees had just handed him.

"Same play again," Levi called, louder this time. "Brodie, deep post."

Brodie looked confused but ran it. Levi came off the screen, and when Asees stepped out to meet him, Levi lobbed the ball over her outstretched hand. Brodie caught it high, turned, and laid it in off the backboard. The little kid in the sandbox clapped like it was a fireworks show.

"See," Levi said, bouncing the ball once. "When you switch, you're on Brodie. That's the mismatch. I just have to find it."

Asees rubbed her chin like a detective. "Run it again, then. But this time I'm not switching."

"Then I'm taking the lane myself," Levi said, and he slapped the ball hard against the pavement.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: In the Sally-Anne test, first used in 1985, children from about age four usually say a character will look where she left her marble, not where it was moved while she was away.
story:
The group chat lit up at 7:42 on a Tuesday night, and Jayden typed fast, because his little cousin was coming over Saturday and he had a plan. "does anyone remember that video Ms. Cruz showed us with the marble and the basket," he wrote. "the Sally-Anne thing from 1985." Charlie-Rose answered first: "the one where the kid says she'll look in the basket?? i thought that was fake." Riya sent a single eye emoji, which meant she was interested but pretending not to be.

"it's not fake," Jayden wrote. "kids from about age four usually say a character will look where she left her marble, not where it was moved while she was away." He explained the setup: Sally-Anne puts her marble in her basket and goes out. While she's gone, someone moves the marble to a box. Then you ask where she'll look. His cousin was three, which meant, if the video was right, she'd probably point at the basket. "i want to try it for real. i need one of you to recruit as the marble mover. saturday, 2pm, my kitchen."

Riya thought it was a strange idea. "isn't that kind of a trick on a three-year-old," she wrote. "you'd basically be setting her up to be wrong." Jayden read the message twice. He hadn't thought of it that way; he mostly wanted to see whether the pattern held with an actual kid he knew, someone who shared his grandmother's laugh and called ducks "quack-quacks." He wrote back, "we make it a game and she gets the marble either way. lots of compassion, zero tricks." Charlie-Rose added, "i'll bring cookies as backup fairness."

Saturday afternoon, the chat filled with photos. Charlie-Rose had hidden the marble in the box while the cousin was in the hallway watching Jayden's dad stir soup. Then the cousin came back, and Jayden asked the question slowly, the way you talk to someone balancing on a curb. "Where will she look for her marble?" The cousin pointed at the basket without hesitating, then ran to check inside it, found nothing, and frowned at the box until Charlie-Rose let her "discover" the marble there, which turned into a game of hiding it four more times.

The last photo showed the cousin asleep on the couch, the marble loose in her fist, and under it Jayden wrote: "basket. she said basket. exactly like the video." Riya replied, "so she thinks people know things they can't know. that's kind of turbulent for a tuesday." Charlie-Rose sent, "she's three. she'll figure out people can be wrong eventually." Jayden set his phone face down on the counter and watched the marble roll a little in his cousin's fingers as she breathed.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Psychologists often separate fear, a reaction to a threat happening now, from anxiety, worry about a threat that might happen in the future.
story:
Ryder pushed his noodles around the plate while his mom talked about Thursday. Basketball tryouts were Thursday, three days away, and his stomach had been sour since Monday morning. He had not eaten much at lunch either. He noticed that, and he noticed something else: whenever Coach Griffin said the word "tryout" in the gym that afternoon, the sour feeling jumped, as if someone had poked it.

"So how was school?" his mom asked.

"Fine," Ryder said. Then, because the word was already on his tongue, he added, "Griffin posted the tryout list."

"That's good, isn't it?"

He shrugged. "It's three days away. Nothing's even happening yet."

After dinner he carried the recycling out and found Mr. Nasser on his porch, sorting seed packets into a shoebox. Mr. Nasser was retired and knew a little about almost everything, including, it turned out, the mind. Ryder mentioned the tryout, and the sour stomach, and how weird it was that a game that did not exist yet could make his body act like it did.

"Ah," Mr. Nasser said. "Psychologists separate fear from anxiety. Fear is a reaction to a threat happening now. Anxiety is worry about a threat that might happen in the future." He held up a seed packet. "Fear is what you feel when a dog is barking at you. Anxiety is what you feel for three days before the dog might bark at you."

Ryder turned that over on the walk back inside. His mom was at the table paying bills, and the quiet ticking of the kitchen clock gave him room to think. So the sick stomach was not about anything real in front of him. It was about a maybe. That meant it might be testable, like the time he and Caelan figured out which locker was rattling by listening at each door in turn.

He sat down across from his mom. "Can I try something?" he asked. "Close your eyes and count to ten with me."

She raised an eyebrow but did it. Ryder closed his eyes too and deliberately pictured the gym on Thursday, the whistle, Griffin with his clipboard, the other boys stretching on the line. His stomach clenched. Then he pictured the gym right now, empty, the lights off, no tryout happening anywhere on Earth at this moment. The sour feeling loosened, just a little, like a knot half undone.

"It's smaller," he said, opening his eyes. "When I make it now instead of later."

His mom said it sounded like he had found a way of coping, and that he should tell her before it turned into cumulative sleep loss instead of just three bad dinners. Ryder laughed. He said Griffin had told the team that a good player adapts to the situation in front of him, and maybe a good stomach did the same thing.

At the table later, doing homework, he wrote a note to Caelan and underlined one line twice: Not a dog yet. Just a maybe dog. When he read it back, he grinned and taped it inside his binder where he would see it Thursday morning.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Stress is the body's response to a demand or challenge, and short bursts of it can help a person focus, such as before a test or a race.
story:
Matteo sat on his bedroom floor with his history notes spread across the carpet, and the chat window on his laptop kept lighting up. Chloe had a piano recital in three days, and she had sent the same message eleven times: "I'm quitting. I have anxiety. Sell my tickets." Jude replied with a random photo of a cat wearing a tiny hat, which was his way of coping, and then added, "You said that before the last recital and you won a medal."

Matteo had his own problem. The chapter test was tomorrow morning, and whenever he thought about it his stomach tightened and his hands went cold. He had been trying to classify the feeling all week: was it the kind that made him want to hide under his desk, or the kind that made him actually sit down and work? He texted Chloe instead of answering her directly. "When you get nervous before you play, does your playing get worse or better?"

She typed for a long time. "Better, I think. I hear every note more. Everything gets sharp."

Matteo stared at the screen. So the tightness in his stomach might not be an enemy. Maybe stress, the body's response to a demand or a challenge, could do something useful, at least in short bursts, the way it sharpened Chloe right before a recital or a runner before a race. He needed to test it. He set a timer for twenty minutes, closed every chat window, and read the chapter straight through. His hands were still cold, but he noticed he wasn't rereading the same sentence four times. The facts stuck. Napoleon, the coal mines, the whole boring parade of dates.

The timer went off and Chloe called him, which broke the boundaries he had just set for himself, but he answered anyway. "I decided I'm not quitting," she said. "But I need you to come Saturday. If I look at you in the second row I won't spiral. Also I need you to hold my backup sheet music, which is a big responsibility, and if you lose it you owe me a piano, no warranty, final sale."

"That's not how warranties work," Matteo said. "Also I can't afford a piano."

"Then don't lose the music."

Jude's message popped up under the call: "I'll be there with the cat hat." Matteo hung up, reset the timer, and opened the chapter again. His stomach still felt tight, but now it felt like a hand on his shoulder, pointing at the page. He read until his mom knocked on the door and told him lights out. He turned off the lamp, put the notes under his pillow like some kind of guarantee, and said to the dark ceiling, "Napoleon, 1812."

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: Computer scientist Scott Fahlman proposed the emoticon :-) on September 19, 1982, on a Carnegie Mellon University message board, so readers could tell which posts were jokes.
story:
The message that ruined Tuesday afternoon was short: "Ms. Chan assigns the most homework of any teacher in the entire school, maybe on Earth." Muhammad had typed it as a joke, but jokes, he was learning, did not always travel well through a screen.

Killian replied first. "Seriously? I'm going to complain to my parents." Then Florence: "Wait, is that real? She gave us that worksheet today, I thought it was reasonable." Within ten minutes the group chat had gone from joking to planning, and Florence had actually started a list of every assignment Ms. Chan had given since September. Muhammad stared at his phone, thumb hovering. Nothing in his message had said "just kidding," because out loud his voice would have done that for him.

He remembered the science trip last spring, when the class stood at the edge of the parking lot while Ms. Chan pointed at the crusty green patches on a stone wall. "That's lichen," she had said. "It looks dormant, but it's alive and working." Then, because a wasp had flown at Killian's head, everyone laughed, and even the teacher smiled, and no one had misunderstood anything, because everyone could see everyone's face. Muhammad thought about how laughter used to arrive at the same time as the words, and how in the chat it seemed to have ceased arriving at all.

He typed: "That was a joke, sorry." Too late, the planning had its own momentum now. Florence had written "Meeting at lunch, we should say something to the principal." Muhammad closed the app, then opened it again, and decided to test an idea: if he could not send his tone, maybe he could type it.

He searched "jokes taken seriously online" and scrolled past forums and articles until he found a page about the very first emoticon. On September 19, 1982, a computer scientist named Scott Fahlman proposed :-) on a Carnegie Mellon University message board so readers could tell which posts were jokes. Muhammad read it twice. Somebody, forty years before he was born, had hit exactly the same problem and solved it with three characters. He copied the little sideways face and pasted it into his message: "Ms. Chan assigns the most homework of any teacher in the entire school, maybe on Earth :-). Also that was a joke. Killing the lunch meeting, please."

Florence replied within a minute. "Oh. I took that completely seriously. Nice face, by the way." Killian sent a row of laughing emojis, and the plan quietly dissolved. Then Florence typed, "Does that thing have a name?" Muhammad answered, "It's called an emoticon," and added a winking one, just to make sure.

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: The first ten amendments to the United States Constitution are called the Bill of Rights, and they were ratified in 1791.
story:
Ruby had until Saturday to stand up in the community centre's main hall and explain one right from the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms in her own words, and so far every attempt had come out sounding like she was reciting a cereal box. Ms. Vogel, who ran the youth rights club on Thursday evenings, had been clear about the rules: no reading from the pamphlet, no copying a definition, just plain words that proved you understood it.

Ruby spread the pamphlet across a wobbly table near the window. She had chosen section 2, the freedom of peaceful assembly, mostly because it sounded less complicated than the legal rights. Dan dropped into the chair across from her, already talking.

"I'm doing the US one," he said. "My grandma lives in Detroit and she mailed me a booklet. She's coming Saturday, and she said she wants to hear me say something true about it." He slid the booklet across the table. "The first ten amendments to the Constitution are called the Bill of Rights, and they were ratified in 1791. Two hundred years before I was born."

"That's extravagant," Ruby said, turning the thin pages. "Two hundred years of people arguing about ten sentences."

She read his amendments and then her Charter section again, and a pattern started to bother her. The American words talked about Congress not making laws against assembly. The Charter said everyone has the freedom. She began to hypothesize that the difference was about who the rule was aimed at: one document told the government what it couldn't do, and the other told people what they could do. She couldn't see it directly, though. It was a guess about a hidden shape.

"I need a test subject," she said. Dan raised his hand immediately, since he wanted the practice anyway. "Don't use the booklet words. Just say it like you'd tell your grandma." She took a breath. "Peaceful assembly means you and other people can stand together in public for something you believe in, as long as you're not hurting anyone or smashing things. The government can't just scatter you because it doesn't like your sign."

Dan frowned, then nodded slowly. "So the rule isn't really about standing. It's about who's allowed to stop you." That was it, exactly the piece she'd been missing, and it had come out of her own mouth before she'd even noticed it was there.

Ms. Vogel paused beside their table on her way past. "Five minutes till we clear the room, and the hall is booked for a birthday party after this, so no lingering." Ruby began gathering the papers, then stopped at Dan's booklet, its corner bent, his grandmother's name written inside the cover in careful blue ink.

"Can I borrow this overnight?" Ruby asked. "I want to read all ten before Saturday."

"Bring it back," Dan said, "or my grandma will ask you about it, and she's more of a quiz than a person."

activity: to use pivot tables in a spreadsheet to summarise survey answers by grade
knowledge_domain: to use pivot tables in a spreadsheet to summarise survey answers by grade
fact: Slicers, clickable buttons that filter a pivot table, were added to Excel in Excel 2010.
story:
Theodore's mother had to postpone her lunch break, so he sat at the empty desk beside hers with his math project spread out: three hundred survey answers about cafeteria food, dumped into a spreadsheet, and no idea how to make sense of them. His table just went on and on, row after row of Grade 6, Grade 7, Grade 8, pizza, pasta, pizza, sushi.

"You're going to type all of that by hand?" said Asma, who had come along to use the office wifi. She leaned over his shoulder. "That's radical levels of boring. Use a pivot table."

"A what?"

She clicked through the menus, dragged Grade into the rows, dragged Food into the columns, and dragged Answer into the values box. The endless table collapsed into a tidy grid: every grade down the side, every food along the top, counts where they crossed. Theodore sat back. It was like watching three hundred students get sorted into seats in one second.

"Okay, that's actually amazing," he said. "But I want to look at just Grade 7 without rebuilding the whole thing."

Asma squinted at the toolbar. "There should be buttons somewhere. I saw them in a video once."

They searched together. Theodore found a button labeled Slicer and clicked it, and a small gray box with three buttons, Grade 6, Grade 7, Grade 8, appeared beside the table. He pressed Grade 7 and the grid narrowed instantly to that one grade. He pressed it again and the full table came back.

The man from the next cubicle wandered over with his coffee. "Careful, that file's old," he said. "Slicers didn't exist before Excel 2010. They were added in 2010. If someone opens that on the ancient version downstairs, the buttons won't be there."

"Then I'll check the version first," Theodore said. He was already pressing Grade 6, then Grade 8, watching the numbers swap in and out. Grade 8 liked sushi almost as much as pizza, which nobody would have guessed from the raw rows.

Ms. Levy, his math teacher, had said the project needed a pattern, not just a pile of answers. Theodore had planned to count by hand all weekend, and he'd told Ireland it would be miserable. Now Ireland texted: still counting? and Theodore sent back a photo of the slicer buttons.

Ireland replied with three question marks.

"Come Monday," Theodore typed, "I'll show you. It's like a network of switches. Press one, the whole table listens."

He dragged Food into the rows instead, just to see what would happen, and the grid rearranged itself again, foods down the side now, grades across the top, still filtered to Grade 8.

"Save it," Asma said, pointing at the screen. "Before your mom's computer eats it."

Theodore hit save and pressed Grade 7 one more time, watching the numbers flicker into place.

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: A paper tissue left in a pocket breaks apart in the wash and scatters white shreds over every item in the load, which is why pockets are checked before washing.
story:
Aaron pushed the grocery cart down the laundry aisle while his dad limped behind him, rubbing his knee. "The cartilage in there is complaining," his dad said, "so you do the reaching." That was fine with Aaron, because the reaching was the whole point. Three days ago he had offered to do his own laundry, a voluntary offer that had seemed like a good idea until he opened the washer and found every one of his dark shirts speckled with tiny white flecks, like snow that had stuck and refused to melt.

He had stared at that load for a long time before he started thinking like a detective. The flecks were soft and thin and tore when he pinched them. Nothing in the machine was white and soft. But his hoodie had a pocket, and when he turned the pocket out, he found the answer: the corner of a paper tissue, the only survivor of the one he had forgotten there. The tissue had broken apart in the wash, he realized, and its shreds had scattered over every single item in the load. That had to be why his mom always checked pockets before washing. Nobody had told him. He had worked it out himself, and now he was here to fix the evidence.

He reached for a bottle of stain remover, then stopped. Would stain remover even work on this? The flecks were not stains, exactly. They were pieces of something sitting on top of the cloth. He put the bottle back and picked up a lint roller instead, rolling the sticky sheet over his own sleeve to test the idea. It lifted fuzz instantly. If the shreds were only clinging to the surface, the roller should pick them up, and the clothes might be fine after a run through the dryer, where the lint trap would catch whatever loosened.

"A lint roller?" said a voice. Ayana from science class was at the end of the aisle, holding a box of dryer sheets. "Laundry emergency?"

"Tissue in a pocket," Aaron said. "One tissue destroyed an entire load of dark clothes."

Ayana winced. "My mom checks every pocket in our house for that exact reason. She found a whole receipt in my dad's jeans once."

"That makes sense," Aaron said. "It's the hidden stuff that gets you." He dropped two lint rollers in the cart, one for now and one for the future.

At the checkout, Mr. Bouchard from next door was ahead of them in line with a small bag of oranges. He glanced at the lint rollers and smiled. "Been there," he said. "My load of black socks looked like a blizzard hit it."

At home, Aaron spread the dark clothes across his bed and rolled, sheet after sticky sheet, until the roller was furred white and his shirts were dark again. He folded them into neat squares, checked every pocket twice, even the empty ones, and stacked them in his drawer. Then he peeled off the used sheet, stuck it to the edge of the trash can, and stood back to admire the pile.

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: A small amount of stress before a test or a game can sharpen focus; stress becomes harmful mainly when it lasts for a long time without relief.
story:
Grandpa's kitchen smelled like toast and chlorine, because Romy had hung her swimsuit over the radiator and it was still damp. She had a swim meet on Saturday, and her stomach had been knotted since Tuesday. She sat at the table, stacked and restacked the jam jars, and could not eat.

"Your hands are going again," Grandpa said, pointing his butter knife at her drumming fingers. "Same as before your music exam."

Romy looked down. He was right. She drummed when something was coming, some deadline or race, and she had never noticed it before. She tried an experiment: she counted the jam jars, breathed in for four counts and out for six, the way the school nurse had shown her class in September, and drummed the table only once more before her hands went still. Her stomach unclenched a little too. Interesting. The jitter had a purpose, she thought, like a warm-up. It arrived before the thing itself and then it left.

That was not true for everyone. Her friend Juno had texted every night for three weeks, saying she felt heavy and could not sleep, kept waking at odd hours, dreading things she could not name. Romy had assumed it was random, but three weeks was not random. Three weeks was a pattern. On Wednesday night Juno came over to Grandpa's, and the two of them built a fort of sofa cushions in the lounge. "The night before a race, my nerves actually help me," Romy said, breathing out slowly. "They sharpen me up. But yours has lasted for weeks. That's different." She got Grandpa's hot water bottle and set a rule: no screens after nine, warm milk, lights out at the same time every night, and ten slow breaths before Juno closed her eyes. Juno fell asleep before the tenth.

On Saturday morning Romy stood on the pool deck in her cap and goggles, and the big crowd did not intimidate her the way it had last season. Her heart hammered, but she recognised it now as the sharp kind, the kind that came and went with the race. She breathed in for four, out for six, and dove clean off the block.

Afterward, dripping, she checked her phone. Juno had slept through the night, twice in a row. And she had done something else: she had written down her worries on a page, found one clear motive behind the heavy feeling, a friendship that had gone wrong at school, and told her mum about it. Romy read the message twice, then typed back, "Grandpa says come Sunday. Bring your own suit."

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: Laughing along with teasing, even just to fit in, signals approval to the person teasing and tends to encourage them to keep going.
story:
The rain had driven everyone inside Rayna's garage, where her dad had set up a ping-pong table and an old space heater that rattled like it was chewing gravel. Gavin was losing, as usual, when Lux started in on a kid from their science class who wasn't even there to defend himself. "Did you see what Marcus wore on the field trip? He looked like a substitute teacher on vacation." Lux grinned and popped a chip in his mouth, then glanced sideways at the group.

Gavin laughed. It was a small laugh, mostly air, the kind you do when you don't want to seem like the one person who didn't get the joke. Rayna laughed too. Lux's grin widened, and he came up with another one, and then a third, each one a little meaner than the last. Gavin noticed something odd: after every joke, Lux looked over at them. Not at Marcus's empty chair, not at the ceiling. At them. It was like the jokes weren't really aimed at Marcus at all; they were aimed at the audience, waiting to see if they landed.

"Wait," Gavin said, mostly to himself. He missed an easy return and let the ball roll under the heater. Lux told another joke, and Gavin watched carefully this time. Joke, then the glance. Joke, then the glance. He began to resent the way he'd been laughing along, because now he could see what his laughing was doing. It wasn't harmless. It was approval, and approval was the mechanism that kept the whole thing running. Every laugh was a little fuel line running straight to Lux.

So Gavin tested it. When the next joke came, he kept his face still and said, "He's actually pretty good at science. He helped me with the volcano write-up." Rayna, catching on, said, "Yeah, mine too." Neither of them laughed. The room went quiet except for the space heater, still chewing its gravel. Lux told one more joke, glancing over hopefully, and when nothing came back he shrugged and started talking about the Raptors game instead. Just like that, the Marcus material dried up.

Later, while they gathered their backpacks, Rayna nudged Gavin with her elbow. "So we're unanimous on this, right? No more laughing at his jokes?" Gavin nodded and zipped his bag. "Unanimous," he agreed. "Although if he starts on the Raptors, I can't make any promises." Lux rolled his eyes and tossed the empty chip bag at the trash can. It bounced off the rim and landed on the floor, and all three of them stared at it for a moment before anyone moved.

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: Section 2 of the Canadian Charter protects fundamental freedoms, including freedom of religion, freedom of expression, freedom of peaceful assembly and freedom of association.
story:
Michael sat on the wooden bench outside courtroom four, holding a photocopy of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms so tightly the pages creased. In twenty minutes, each student in Ms. Leung's civics class had to stand up in the courtroom, which a judge had lent them for the morning, and explain one right in their own words. Michael had drawn fundamental freedoms. He had read the section six times on the bus and still could not say it out loud without stumbling.

"Which one did you get?" Diana asked, dropping onto the bench beside him.

"Section 2," Michael said. "Fundamental freedoms. There are four of them, and every time I try to list them I leave one out. My reflex is to say religion, expression, and then I panic and say 'the one about hanging out with people.'"

"That's assembly," said Mavrik from the floor, where he was flipping through his own pages. "Peaceful assembly. We used it last month when the city tried to thwart our little demonstration about the park closing. Ms. Leung showed us the exact section." He held up his paper. "Also association. You can belong to a group. So: religion, expression, assembly, association."

Michael tested it under his breath. Religion, expression, assembly, association. He tried it backwards. Association, assembly, expression, religion. He wrote the four words on his hand, then crossed them out, because writing on his hand felt like cheating even though nobody had said it was. "Okay," he said. "But I have to explain one, not just list them. What do I actually say about expression?"

"Say something true," Diana said. "Like, you can say what you think. Even if nobody likes it. Even if it's about the cafeteria meatloaf."

"That," Mavrik said, "is the bravest use of free expression anyone has attempted in this courthouse."

Inside, the courtroom smelled like dust and old carpet. Ms. Leung stood by the bar with her clipboard, and when Michael's name was called he walked to the front, took a breath, and said, "Section 2 of the Charter protects fundamental freedoms. Freedom of religion, freedom of expression, freedom of peaceful assembly, and freedom of association." He paused. All four. None missing. "Expression means you can say what you actually think. Peaceful means without breaking stuff, which our demonstration about the park did not, mostly because Mavrik brought cookies instead of a megaphone."

Two rows back, Mavrik raised the cookie tin like evidence.

Ms. Leung wrote something on her clipboard, then looked up. "Clear, accurate, and assertive. Nicely done, Michael."

Walking out through the heavy front doors, Diana nudged him. "Meatloaf was risky."

"Freedom of expression," Michael said, and held the door.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Pressing guitar strings repeatedly makes the fingertips sore at first; with regular practice, the skin toughens into calluses and playing hurts less.
story:
Lauren sat on her grandmother's porch with the borrowed guitar across her lap and pressed her left fingertips against the strings. Each press stung. She had been practicing for one week, exactly seven days, and the tips of her fingers were sore and red, and she was ready to put the guitar back in its case for good.

"I thought you wanted to learn a song for the spring concert," said Vanessa, who had come over to watch and was sitting on the porch rail.

"I did. But it hurts every time I press a string. Look." Lauren held out her hand. "I can't even do a chord for a whole song."

Vanessa was indifferent to the red fingers. She had never played anything and didn't think a little soreness was much of a story. "Alice's brother plays. Ask him. Or just quit."

Lauren didn't answer. She looked at the guitar and thought about something her grandmother had said at breakfast, about how her hands had changed after years of kneading bread, the skin on her palms thick where the dough pressed hardest. Skin changed, then, when something pressed on it over and over. Maybe that was a rule that worked the same way for fingers and strings. If so, the soreness wasn't a reason to stop. It was a stage, and the stage had an exit.

She decided to run a test on herself. She would practice a little every single day for two more weeks and keep a chart on the refrigerator door, marking each day and whether the strings still hurt. If nothing changed by the end, she would quit and the chart would be her testimony, proof she had really tried.

Vanessa tried to delegate the job of tracking the chart to Alice, who arrived on day four with lemonade and no interest in charts. "You made the plan, you mark it," Alice said. "I'm just here for the lemonade." So Lauren did it herself, drawing a small guitar on each square.

The first few days, the strings still bit. On day eight, a chord felt slightly less sharp. On day eleven, Lauren noticed the skin on her fingertips had grown harder, rough pads where the strings landed. She pressed a string and held it down for a long count, and it barely hurt at all.

"Grandma," she said, holding out her hand on the porch that evening, "feel this."

Her grandmother ran a thumb over the fingertips. "Calluses," she said.

On day fourteen, Lauren marked the last square on the chart, then set the chart aside, placed her fingers on the strings, and played the first line of the song all the way through.

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: A settler's diary shows one person's view; it rarely tells how the Native American nations whose lands the trails crossed saw the same events.
story:
Avery slid the microfiche machine aside, which nobody had used since approximately the dawn of time, and spread her materials across the library table like a detective in a movie. Her task, assigned by Mr. Shevchenko, was to use a primary source to explain why people moved west in the 1800s. She had chosen a settler's diary, photocopies of it anyway, and she'd read the same page four times.

"Fourth read," said Lexi, dropping into the chair across from her. "That's dedication. Or a cry for help."

"It's good," Avery said. "Listen. He writes, 'The land is empty and waiting, and we shall have a fine farm by spring.'" She tapped the page. "That's why they moved. Land. Mr. Shevchenko will love it."

Mercedes arrived with two granola bars and zero subtlety. "He'll love the first half of that sentence," she said, unwrapping one.

Avery frowned. "What's wrong with the first half?"

"The land is empty," Mercedes quoted, wiggling her eyebrows. "Empty. To whom?"

Sunlight came through the tall library windows and refracted through the glass tabletop, laying a crooked rainbow across the photocopies. Avery moved her page out of the rainbow and then moved it back, because it looked cool, and then actually thought about what Mercedes had said. The diary said the land was empty and waiting. She tried to imagine who else might have been standing on that same prairie on the same day, watching the wagon roll in.

She flipped through the rest of the photocopies. Farmers, rivers, a broken axle, a fever, stamina praised in old-timey spelling. It was all one man, one pair of eyes, the whole way through. The trails in the back of her textbook crossed land that belonged to Native American nations, and those nations had seen the same wagons arrive. She checked the diary again anyway, in case the man had thought about that even once. He hadn't. A settler's diary shows one person's view, she realized; it rarely tells how the people already living on that land saw the same events.

"So what do I do?" Avery said. "My source is half a pair of glasses."

"Then say so," Lexi said. "Quote him, then point out the other half is missing. That's not cheating, that's thinking."

Avery pulled a fresh note card toward her and wrote, in her most confident handwriting, "Source shows one view. The view from the other side of the fence is not in this book." Then she wrote a second card, a silly one: "The prairie was not actually waiting. The prairie was busy."

Mercedes read it over her shoulder and snorted granola. Mr. Shevchenko passed behind them on his endless slow lap of the library, paused, read the cards upside down, and said nothing, which for him was a standing ovation.

"He stopped," Lexi whispered. "He never stops."

"He stopped," Avery agreed, and angled the note card so the rainbow landed right on it.
